judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the 'All categories' radio (#categoryAll). Its aria-labelledby points to the legend 'Category', so its computed name is 'Category' (the CDP tree confirms nameFrom aria-labelledby), and that word alone does not identify this option, so the sentence holds of the capture. For 2.4.6, though, WCAG's glossary separates a label (presented to all users) from a name (which may be exposed only to assistive technology). The labels users see are the visible <label for> 'All categories' and the legend 'Category' for the group, which are descriptive on a search form for inspection reports (screenshot checked). The real defect is that aria-labelledby overrides the option's own label: the name lacks the visible label (2.5.3, reported separately; arguably 4.1.2/1.3.1 as well), not a non-descriptive label. The live HTML, fetched with a browser user agent, has the same markup, and the screenshot is fully styled. So the capture does not differ.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The 'All categories' radio (#categoryAll) has a visible <label for="categoryAll">All categories</label> next to it (screenshot), but aria-labelledby="category" overrides that label, and the CDP accessible name is 'Category'. 'All categories' is not contained in 'Category'. This is failure F96 of 2.5.3: a speech user saying 'click All categories' gets no match, and 'Category' matches all five radios. I looked for a reason it passes and found none. No exception applies, the label is the radio's own visible text label, and the live HTML has the same aria-labelledby on the radio, so the capture does not differ. The claim names exactly this failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The element is the header logo image (img src /images/logo.svg, alt 'Ofsted Logo') inside the home link, alongside visually hidden text 'Ofsted homepage'. The crop and the screenshot show the Ofsted logo: the wordmark 'Ofsted' with three small figures above it. So the alternative describes exactly what the image shows, and the claim is false. Under 1.1.1 the alternative identifies the logo and conveys its text. Including the word 'Logo', and repeating the link text, are style points, not a failure. The live HTML has the same img and alt, so the capture does not differ.
